title: Structs, Enums & Pattern Matching
summary: Model ships, cargo and orders as your own types. Add methods with impl, let enums carry data, and take them apart with exhaustive match, guards, if let and let else, without moving out of borrowed values.

quest.title: The Shipwright's Blueprints
quest.story:
The Crab Fleet has grown. There are ships with names and crews, holds full of rum, gold and treasure maps, and the captain barks a dozen kinds of orders a day. The old quartermaster tracked all of it in loose strings and numbers, and nobody can tell a barrel count from a cannon count anymore.

The fleet's shipwright hands you a set of blueprints: **structs** to build ships from, **enums** to say exactly which kind of cargo or order you are holding, and **match** to read them back. *Rustc* the parrot has learned a new trick too. Forget one kind of order in a `match` and it squawks before the ship ever leaves port.

Draw up the blueprints, teach the ships to obey orders, and the shipwright will sign you on as the fleet's master builder.

concepts.title: Three kinds of struct
concepts.body:
A **struct** groups named values into one new type. Each field is owned by the struct, so dropping the struct drops its fields.

```rust
struct Ship {          // named fields
    name: String,
    guns: u32,
}
struct Doubloons(u32); // tuple struct: fields by position, .0
struct Calm;           // unit struct: no data at all

let pearl = Ship { name: String::from("Pearl"), guns: 8 };
let purse = Doubloons(30);
println!("{} has {} guns and {} coins", pearl.name, pearl.guns, purse.0);
```

Tuple structs give a plain number its own type, so a `Doubloons` can never be mixed up with a crew count. Unit structs are useful as markers.

Add `#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]` above a type to get `{:?}` printing, `.clone()` and `==` for free. Each derive only works if every field supports it too.

concepts.title: impl blocks: methods and associated functions
Enums carry data
concepts.body:
An **enum** value is exactly *one* of its variants, and each variant can carry its own data:

```rust
enum Cargo {
    Rum(u32),                 // tuple-like variant
    Map(String),              // owns a heap String
    Chest { gold: u32 },      // struct-like variant
    Empty,                    // no data
}
```

In memory an enum is a small **tag** that says which variant it is, plus enough room for the largest variant. A `Cargo::Map` holds the String's pointer, length and capacity inline, and the text itself lives on the heap.

`Option<T>` (`Some(T)` or `None`) and `Result<T, E>` are ordinary enums from the standard library.

concepts.title: match is exhaustive
concepts.body:
`match` compares a value against patterns from top to bottom and runs the first arm that fits. It must cover **every** possible value, or rustc stops with **E0004** (non-exhaustive patterns):

```rust
let worth = match cargo {
    Cargo::Rum(n) if n > 100 => n * 3,   // binding + guard
    Cargo::Rum(n) => n * 2,              // n is bound to the data
    Cargo::Chest { gold } => gold,       // struct-variant field
    Cargo::Map(_) | Cargo::Empty => 0,   // _ ignores, | combines
};
```

- A **guard** (`if ...`) only adds a condition. It does not count towards exhaustiveness, so you still need an unguarded arm.
- `..` skips the remaining fields: `Ship { name, .. }`.
- Prefer naming every variant over a catch-all `_`. Then adding a new variant later makes rustc point at every `match` that must handle it.

concepts.title: if let and let else
Matching through a borrow: E0507, & and ref

visual.title: A ship, its cargo, and a borrowing match

steps.note: A struct is its fields laid side by side on the stack: name is a String (pointer, length, capacity) and guns is a plain u32.
hold is an enum: a tag saying Map, plus room for the largest variant. The Map variant owns its own heap String.
match &hold looks at the tag through a shared reference. Nothing is moved, so hold is frozen but not taken.
The Map arm matches. Because we matched on &hold, place binds as &String: a borrow of the data inside hold, not a move.
The arm ends, place goes away, and hold is fully usable again. Without the &, place would have tried to move the String out of hold.
You can also borrow a single field. flag points at ship.name only, and ship.guns stays free to use.
End of main: hold and ship are dropped, and each drops the String it owns. Both heap buffers are freed exactly once.

challenges.title: The forgotten order
challenges.story: The bosun wrote a function that turns orders into shouts. The crew only ever hears "hoist the sails!", so surely nobody will notice the gap.
challenges.prompt: Read the program. What happens when you compile and run it?

choices.label: It prints `hoist the sails!`: `Fire` is never used, so the missing arm doesn't matter
Compile error E0004: non-exhaustive patterns, `Order::Fire` not covered
It compiles, but would panic at runtime if `shout(Order::Fire)` were ever called
It compiles with only a warning: variant `Fire` is never constructed

hints: Does rustc check `match` arms at compile time, or does it wait to see which values actually arrive?
A `match` must handle every value the type can have, whether or not your program ever creates it.
`Order::Fire` has no arm, so this is the non-exhaustive match error, E0004. Fix it with a `Order::Fire => ...` arm.

challenges.title: Hiring hands
challenges.story: The shipwright's first blueprint: a ship that can hire crew and describe itself. Each method grabbed the wrong kind of `self`, and now the ship either can't change or vanishes after one look.
challenges.prompt:
This program does not compile. Fix the **methods** so it compiles and prints exactly:

```text
Pearl with 5 crew
Pearl with 7 crew
```

Rules:
- Do not change `main` or the `Ship` struct.
- No `.clone()`.
- Only change the receivers (`self`, `&self`, `&mut self`) of the methods, and nothing else in their bodies.
hints: There are two separate problems. Read each error: one is about changing a field, the other about using `ship` after it was moved.
`hire` changes a field, so it needs a receiver that allows mutation. `describe` only reads, so it must not take ownership.
Use `fn hire(&mut self, n: u32)` and `fn describe(&self) -> String`.

cases.name: hires twice and describes twice
cases.expected:
Pearl with 5 crew
Pearl with 7 crew

forbid.message: No .clone(): pick the right receiver instead of copying the ship.

require.message: hire changes the ship, so it should take &mut self.
describe only reads the ship, so it should take &self.

challenges.title: Sorting the hold
challenges.story: The cook sorts the hold with a `match`. He swears big rum casks are for parties only.

choices.label: Compile error: `n` can't be bound in two variants of one arm
Compile error E0004: the guard makes the match non-exhaustive

hints: Arms are tried top to bottom, and only the **first** arm that fits runs. There is no fall-through.
A guard only adds a condition to its arm. `Rum(3)` fails the guard and moves on to the next arm. An or-pattern may bind `n` in both alternatives as long as the types match.
Rum(12) hits the guarded arm, Gold(2) and Rum(3) print their numbers, and Empty prints `nothing`.

challenges.title: Don't steal the map
challenges.story: The harbour master only *looks* at each ship's papers, but the description function tries to walk off with the treasure map. *Rustc* squawks: "cannot move out of a shared reference!"
challenges.prompt:
This program does not compile. Make it compile and print exactly:

```text
Pearl carries 12 barrels of rum
Gull carries a map to Skull Isle
Wren sails empty
3 ships in the harbour
```

Rules:
- `describe` must keep the signature `fn describe(ship: &Ship) -> String`.
- Do not change `main`, `Ship` or `Cargo`.
- No `.clone()`. Borrow the map instead of moving it.
hints: Read error E0507: which arm tries to *move* something, and why isn't `describe` allowed to move it?
`ship` is only borrowed. The `Rum(n)` arm is fine because `u32` is `Copy`, but `Map(place)` would move the `String` out of the ship.
Match on a reference, `match &ship.hold { ... }`, so `place` becomes a `&String`. Writing `Cargo::Map(ref place)` works too.

cases.name: describes the whole fleet
cases.expected:
Pearl carries 12 barrels of rum
Gull carries a map to Skull Isle
Wren sails empty
3 ships in the harbour

forbid.message: No .clone(): borrow the map with & or ref instead of copying it.

require.message: Keep the signature fn describe(ship: &Ship) -> String.

challenges.title: Blueprint for a cargo ship
challenges.story: The shipwright has drawn the outline of a cargo ship. Fill in the methods so it can load, count, find and finally be scuttled for its maps.
challenges.prompt:
Fill in every `todo!()` in the `impl Ship` block. The types are given:

- `Ship::new(name: &str) -> Ship`: a ship with that name and an empty hold.
- `load(&mut self, cargo: Cargo)`: put the cargo at the end of the hold.
- `rum(&self) -> u32`: total barrels over all `Cargo::Rum` entries.
- `gold(&self) -> Doubloons`: total of all `Cargo::Gold` entries, wrapped in the tuple struct `Doubloons`.
- `first_map(&self) -> Option<&str>`: the place of the **first** `Cargo::Map` in the hold, or `None`.
- `scuttle(self) -> Vec<String>`: consume the ship and return the places of all its maps, in hold order, **moved out** of the hold.

No `.clone()` anywhere: `first_map` borrows, and `scuttle` owns the ship and can move. Hidden tests call each method directly.
hints: `new` builds a `Ship { ... }` literal; `Vec::new()` is an empty hold. `load` pushes onto `self.hold`.
To look at each entry without taking it, loop over `&self.hold`. Then `if let Cargo::Rum(n) = cargo` binds `n` as `&u32`, and `total += n` still works.

`first_map` can `return Some(place)` from inside `if let Cargo::Map(place) = cargo` (a `&String` coerces to `&str`). `scuttle` owns `self`, so `for cargo in self.hold` gives owned `Cargo` values and `Map(place)` moves the `String` out.

forbid.message: No .clone(): borrow in first_map, move in scuttle.

challenges.title: Call out the orders
challenges.story: The captain's orders arrive as values of the `Order` enum. The lookout needs one function that turns any order into the words he shouts from the crow's nest.
challenges.prompt:
The `Order` enum is given. Write `fn call_out(order: &Order) -> String` that returns:

- `Sail` with `knots` 0: `drift toward {heading}`
- `Sail` with `knots` 20 or more: `full speed to {heading}!`
- any other `Sail`: `sail to {heading} at {knots} knots`
- `Fire` with `guns` 0: `hold fire`
- `Fire` with `guns` 1: `fire 1 gun`
- any other `Fire`: `fire {guns} guns`
- `Signal` with an empty string: `(silence)`
- any other `Signal`: `signal: {text}`
- `Anchor`: `drop anchor`

Here `{heading}`, `{knots}`, `{guns}` and `{text}` stand for the order's data.

Examples: `Order::Sail { heading: String::from("Tortuga"), knots: 8 }` gives `sail to Tortuga at 8 knots`, and `Order::Fire { guns: 3 }` gives `fire 3 guns`.

Rules: take the order by reference and don't clone it. Keep a `fn main()`; it can call `call_out` or stay empty.

After the tests pass, the tutor judges whether your matching is idiomatic.
hints: One `match order { ... }` with an arm per case reads best. Arms are tried top to bottom, so put the special cases first.
Struct-like variants destructure by field name: `Order::Fire { guns: 0 }` matches a literal, `Order::Fire { guns }` binds it. A guard like `if *knots >= 20` handles ranges.

Because `order` is a `&Order`, bindings such as `heading` and `text` are references. Use them directly in `format!("drift toward {heading}")`, no clone needed. Use `if text.is_empty()` as a guard for the silent signal.

forbid.message: No .clone(): bindings from matching on &Order are already references you can format.

challenges.rubric: Idiomatic matching: a single match on the borrowed order (match order { ... } relying on match ergonomics, or match *order with ref bindings) with one arm per case. Struct-like variants are destructured by field name (Order::Sail { heading, knots }), literal patterns are used for exact values (knots: 0, guns: 0, guns: 1), and guards (if *knots >= 20, if text.is_empty()) handle conditions. Every variant is named explicitly; no catch-all _ arm over the enum's variants, so adding a variant later is a compile error. Bindings are used by reference: no .clone(), .to_owned() or .to_string() on fields just to get ownership. Deduct points for if/else chains comparing fields after the match, nested matches where a guard or literal pattern would do, accessing fields through extra helper methods instead of patterns, matches!/== tests on the whole enum, unwrap, or duplicated format strings. A plain String::from or .to_string() for fixed messages is fine.

challenges.title: Boss: The Captain's Order Book
challenges.story: The captain drops the order book on your desk. Every line is an order for the *Crab Queen*, and the program that should carry them out is half built and won't compile. Make the ship obey and the shipwright's seal is yours.
challenges.prompt:
The program reads one order per line from stdin, applies each to the ship *Crab Queen* (starting in port `Tortuga`), prints one log line per order, and ends with a report. Complete it:

1. Implement `describe`, `parse_order` and the missing arms of `Ship::apply`.
2. Fix `Ship::report`, which does not compile.

**Input.** Each line is trimmed and blank lines are skipped. A line is split on whitespace and must be exactly one of these (case-sensitive, `N` is a `u32`):

```text
load rum N     load gold N     load map PLACE
sail PLACE     fire N          unload
```

Anything else, such as unknown words, extra or missing words, or a bad number, is invalid and prints `? ` followed by the trimmed line.

**Log lines** from `apply` (`describe` gives `N rum`, `N gold` or `map to PLACE`):

- load: `loaded <describe>`
- sail: `already in PLACE` if the ship is already there, else `sailed to PLACE` and the port changes
- fire: `held fire` for 0, else `fired N` (shots are added up)
- unload: removes the **last** cargo and prints `unloaded <describe>`, or `hold is empty`

**Report**, always the last line:

```text
Crab Queen in Havana | rum 12 | gold 5 | maps 0 | shots 3
```

Rules: keep the given types and `main`, and no `.clone()`. Hidden cases include an empty order book, invalid lines and unloading an empty hold.
hints: Start with the compile errors: rustc lists the order variants that `apply` doesn't cover (E0004), and `report` tries to move the hold out of a borrowed ship (E0507).

In `report`, loop over `&self.hold`. In `apply`, a guard `Order::Sail(place) if place == self.port` handles the "already there" case before the general `Sail` arm. `self.hold.pop()` returns an `Option<Cargo>`.
For `parse_order`, collect the words into a `Vec<&str>` and match on `words.as_slice()` with slice patterns like `["load", "rum", n]` and `["unload"]`, plus `_ => return None`.

Parse numbers with let else: `let Ok(n) = n.parse() else { return None; };`. A place becomes owned with `place.to_string()`. In the `Sail` arm, build the log line first, then move `place` into `self.port`.

forbid.message: No .clone(): borrow with & where you only look, and move where you own.

cards.front: Name the three kinds of struct and how you read their fields.
cards.back: **Named**: `struct Ship { name: String }`, read with `ship.name`. **Tuple**: `struct Doubloons(u32)`, read with `.0`. **Unit**: `struct Calm;`, which has no fields at all.

cards.front: When does a method take `&self`, `&mut self` or `self`?
cards.back: `&self` to only read, `&mut self` to change fields, `self` to **consume** the value (the caller can't use it afterwards). Pick the weakest one that works. A function in an `impl` with no `self` (like `new`) is an *associated function*, called as `Ship::new(...)`.

cards.front: What is E0004, and why does it fire even if a variant is never used?
cards.back: **Non-exhaustive patterns**: a `match` doesn't cover every value of the type. rustc checks this at compile time from the type, not from the values your program happens to create. Add the missing arm, ideally naming the variant instead of using `_`.

cards.front: `Rum(n) if n > 10 => ...` is followed by `Rum(n) => ...`. What happens to `Rum(3)`?
cards.back: The guard fails, so matching continues with the next arm and `Rum(3)` takes the unguarded `Rum(n)` arm. Arms are tried top to bottom, only the first match runs, and guards don't count towards exhaustiveness.

cards.front: `fn f(s: &Ship)` with `match s.hold { Cargo::Map(p) => ... }` fails with E0507. Why, and what are the fixes?
cards.back: Binding `p` would **move** the `String` out of a value you only borrow. Match on a reference instead, `match &s.hold`, so `p` becomes a `&String`, or write `Cargo::Map(ref p)`. Copy data like `u32` bindings is fine either way.

cards.front: When do you use `if let` instead of `match`?
cards.back: When only one pattern matters and everything else is ignored: `if let Cargo::Map(place) = cargo { ... }`. It skips the boilerplate `_ => {}` arm.

cards.front: What does `let Ok(n) = s.parse::<u32>() else { return None; };` do?
cards.back: If the pattern matches, `n` is bound for the **rest of the block**. Otherwise the `else` block runs, and it must diverge (`return`, `break`, `continue` or panic). It keeps the happy path flat.

cards.front: What do you get from `#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]` on a struct or enum?
cards.back: `Debug` enables `{:?}` printing, `Clone` gives `.clone()` (a deep copy), and `PartialEq` gives `==` and `!=`, which `assert_eq!` needs. A derive only works if every field implements that trait too.
